title: Keeping food safe: why food goes bad, and how to stop it

summary.text: Dal left out on a hot day turns sour and frothy by the next morning. Tiny living beings called microbes got into it, ate it and multiplied. Washing and covering keep microbes out of food. Cooking kills most of them, and a cold fridge slows the rest. Drying, salt, sugar and sourness keep food for months, which is how pickles and vadams last.
summary.art: Three steel dabbas of dal water on a kitchen shelf: one closed, one open with a fly near it, one closed with a green leaf inside, and a girl with a notebook looking at them.

intro.hook: Smell a spoon of fresh curd, then a spoon of curd left out for two days. What changed? Nobody added anything to it.
intro.text: Nothing was added that you could see. But food is never empty of life. Tiny living beings called microbes land on it from the air, from hands and from other food. In warm food they eat and multiply, and that is what you smell. In this unit you find out how families keep food safe, and you test it with three dabbas of dal water.
intro.art: A child holding two spoons of curd, one fresh and smooth, one older with a sour, watery look, sniffing from a little distance.

outcomes: I can say why food goes bad: microbes land on it, eat it and multiply.
I can explain how washing, covering, cooking and cooling each help keep food safe.
I can explain why time matters: a few microbes double again and again until there are millions.
I can run a fair test with three dabbas of dal water and use my results to explain which stayed fresh longest.
I can name the main parts of food (carbohydrates, proteins, fats, vitamins and minerals, fibre and water) and say the job of each.
I can explain how drying, salt, sugar, oil and sourness keep foods like pickles and vadams for a long time.
I can test a food-safety idea, like the five-second rule, and say whether the evidence supports it.

terms.meaning: A living being too small to see without a microscope. Bacteria, moulds and yeasts are microbes.
terms.example: The bacteria that turn milk into curd are microbes.
terms.art: A spoon of curd with a zoomed-in circle showing tiny rod-shaped bacteria.

terms.meaning: Microbes made of just one tiny cell each. One of them is called a bacterium. They live almost everywhere.
terms.example: Bacteria in warm dal can make it sour and frothy by the next morning.
terms.art: A drop of dal under a magnifying circle, with many tiny rod and ball shapes.

terms.meaning: A kind of fungus that grows as fine threads on food, often making green, white or black fuzzy spots.
terms.example: The green fuzz on an old piece of bread is mould.
terms.art: A slice of bread with a round green fuzzy patch, and a zoomed-in view of thin threads.

terms.meaning: A tiny, tough resting cell made by some bacteria and moulds. Spores survive drying and even boiling, and start growing again when things get better.
terms.example: Mould spores float in the air of every kitchen and land on food.
terms.art: Tiny round spores drifting through the air above a kitchen counter.

terms.meaning: To grow in number. A bacterium multiplies by splitting into two.
terms.example: One bacterium becomes 2, then 4, then 8, in warm food.
terms.art: One small round cell splitting into two, then four.

terms.meaning: When food goes bad because microbes are growing in it. Spoiled food may smell sour, froth, go slimy or grow fuzz.
terms.example: Sambar left out overnight in summer can spoil.
terms.art: A bowl of sambar with bubbles on top and a wrinkled-nose child at a distance.

terms.meaning: An illness that comes from eating food with harmful microbes, or the poisons they make, in it. It can cause vomiting and loose motions.
terms.example: Eating cut fruit that sat uncovered in the sun all day can give you food poisoning.
terms.art: A child lying on a sofa holding a glass of ORS, with a worried parent beside her.

terms.meaning: To get harmful microbes or dirt into something clean. Unwashed hands, flies and raw meat can contaminate food.
terms.example: A fly that walks on rubbish and then on your idli contaminates it.
terms.art: A housefly stepping from a dustbin lid onto a plate of idli, with tiny dots on their feet.

terms.meaning: To heat a food like milk for a short time, then cool it quickly, so most of its microbes die.
terms.example: Packet milk in India is pasteurised before it reaches the shop.
terms.art: A milk packet with a small picture of milk moving through a hot pipe and then a cold one.

terms.meaning: To keep food from spoiling for a long time, for example by drying it, salting it, or pickling it.
terms.example: Lemon pickle in salt keeps for many months.
terms.art: A glass jar of yellow lemon pickle and a steel plate of sun-dried vadams on a balcony.

terms.meaning: When microbes we want change a food in a useful way, for example making it sour or making it rise.
terms.example: Idli batter ferments overnight and rises.
terms.art: A steel vessel of idli batter that has risen to the top overnight.

terms.meaning: A part of food that the body needs to live, grow and stay well. Carbohydrates, proteins, fats, vitamins and minerals are nutrients.
terms.example: Dal gives you protein, and rice gives you carbohydrate.
terms.art: A thali with small labels pointing to the rice, dal, ghee, vegetables and curd.

terms.meaning: The part of food that gives the body most of its energy. Starch and sugar are carbohydrates.
terms.example: Rice, ragi, chapati and potatoes are full of carbohydrate.
terms.art: A plate with rice, a ragi ball, a chapati and a boiled potato.

terms.meaning: The part of food the body uses to build and repair itself, such as new skin and muscle.
terms.example: Dal, milk, paneer, eggs and fish are rich in protein.
terms.art: A bowl of dal, a glass of milk, an egg and a piece of fish.

terms.meaning: The rough part of plant food that the body does not digest. It helps food move through the gut.
terms.example: The skin of a guava and whole moong are full of fibre.
terms.art: A cut guava and a handful of whole green moong.

explanations.definition: Food spoils when microbes such as bacteria and moulds land on it, feed on it and multiply.
explanations.description: Microbes are everywhere: in the air, on hands, on vegetables and in soil. When some land on food that is warm and wet, they feed on it. As they feed, they make gases and acids. That is why spoiled dal smells sour and froths, and why old bread grows fuzz. Food also changes in other ways, without microbes. A cut apple turns brown in air, and old oil can smell stale.
examples: Dal left out overnight in summer smells sour and has bubbles on top.
A green fuzzy spot grows on bread kept in a closed bag for a week.
Milk left out on a hot day turns sour and lumpy.
explanations.art: A drop of dal under a zoom circle, with bacteria feeding and splitting, and tiny gas bubbles rising.
explanations.context: This card explains what is really happening when food goes bad.

explanations.concept: A microbe's own problem: finding a meal
explanations.definition: Like every living being, a microbe needs food, water and warmth to live and multiply.
explanations.description: Look at life from a microbe's side. They are too small to walk to food, so they must land on it, carried by air, water, hands or flies. Then they need water to soak up food, and warmth to grow fast. Our cooked food has all three, so it is a perfect home for them. When times are hard, some bacteria and moulds make spores. A spore is a tough resting cell that can wait through drying or boiling, and grow again later.
examples: Bacteria in a dry packet of poha cannot grow, because there is no water.
Mould spores floating in the kitchen air wait until they land on damp bread.
Some spores survive boiling, which is why cooked rice and dal can still spoil if left warm.
explanations.art: A tiny bacterium drifting on a speck of dust towards a warm bowl of rice, with drops of water and wavy warm lines.
explanations.context: This card looks at food from the microbes' side: what they need, and how spores help them wait.

explanations.concept: From a few to millions: why time matters
explanations.definition: Bacteria multiply by splitting in two, so their number doubles again and again.
explanations.description: In warm food, some bacteria can split every 20 minutes. One becomes 2, then 4, then 8. After 2 hours there can be 64, and after 7 hours more than 2 million. So a food with a few microbes is usually safe, but the same food left warm for hours may not be. The World Health Organization says cooked food should not sit at room temperature for more than 2 hours.
examples: Idli batter rises overnight because its microbes multiply for hours.
Cooked food eaten within 2 hours is safer than the same food eaten in the evening.
A fridge does not kill bacteria, but it slows their splitting a lot.
explanations.art: A clock face with a few dots at 1 o'clock, more at 3, and a crowd of dots at 7.
explanations.context: This card explains why a few microbes in food become a problem only after time.

explanations.concept: Washing and covering: keeping microbes out
explanations.definition: Washing moves microbes and dirt off food and hands. Covering stops new microbes landing on food.
explanations.description: Soil on vegetables carries many microbes. Washing in running water and rubbing with your fingers moves much of that soil and its microbes away. Washing does not remove every microbe, so food eaten raw must be washed well. Covering food keeps off dust, flies and drops from a cough. A fly walks on rubbish and then on food, carrying microbes on their feet and mouth.
examples: Coriander from the market is washed until the water stays clear.
A net cover or a steel plate keeps flies off a plate of hot idli.
Hands are washed with soap before cooking and before eating.
explanations.art: A girl rinsing coriander under a tap into a steel bowl, and a steel plate covering a vessel of rice beside her.
explanations.context: This card explains two of the food-safety habits: washing and covering.

explanations.concept: Cooking and cooling: killing microbes or slowing them
explanations.definition: Heat kills most microbes. Cold slows them down. Neither works if food then sits warm for hours.
explanations.description: Boiling water is 100 degrees Celsius. At that heat most bacteria die within a minute or two. A pressure cooker gets hotter, about 120 degrees, and kills even more. Spores and some poisons that microbes make can survive boiling. So cooking helps most when food is eaten soon, or cooled and put in the fridge. A fridge should be colder than 5 degrees Celsius. Microbes grow fastest between 5 and 60 degrees.
examples: Milk is boiled, then covered, to keep it from going sour.
Leftover sambar is cooled, covered and put in the fridge.
Chicken and eggs are cooked until no pink or runny part is left.
explanations.art: A thermometer drawn as a tall column: hot zone at the top with a boiling pot, a red danger band in the middle, and a fridge at the bottom.
explanations.context: This card explains the other two habits: cooking and keeping food cold.

explanations.concept: Keep raw and cooked food apart
explanations.definition: Raw meat, fish, eggs and unwashed vegetables can carry microbes onto cooked food that is ready to eat.
explanations.description: Cooking kills the microbes in the food being cooked. But if raw fish touches a board, and cooked food is then cut on the same board, microbes ride across. The World Health Organization calls this one of its five keys to safer food. Use a separate board and knife, or wash them with soap and hot water in between.
examples: Raw fish is cut on one board, and the cucumber salad on another.
A plate that held raw chicken is washed before cooked chicken goes on it.
Raw eggs are kept in their own box in the fridge.
explanations.art: Two chopping boards side by side: one with raw fish, one with cucumber slices, with a cross on an arrow between them.
explanations.context: This card is about a fifth habit: keeping raw and cooked food apart.

explanations.concept: Old ways of keeping food: drying, salt, sugar, oil and sourness
explanations.definition: Food keeps for a long time when microbes cannot get water, or when it is too salty, too sweet or too sour for most of them.
explanations.description: Microbes need water. Sun-dried vadams, appalams and dried fish keep for months, because there is almost no water left in them. Lots of salt or sugar pulls water out of microbes, so they cannot grow. That is how lemon pickle and mango jam keep. Sour foods, such as tamarind and lemon, slow down many microbes too. In pickles, a layer of oil on top also keeps air and new microbes off. A wet spoon can bring water into a pickle and let mould grow.
examples: Tamarind rice was a favourite food for long train journeys.
Kerala families dry fish in the sun and store it for the rainy months.
Families in the north make aam papad, thin sheets of dried mango pulp.
explanations.art: A sunny balcony with vadams drying on a cloth, a jar of lemon pickle, and a string of dried red chillies.
explanations.context: This card explains how families kept food for months, long before fridges.

explanations.concept: Spoiling and fermenting: microbes we do not want, and microbes we do
explanations.definition: Fermenting is when microbes we want change food in a useful way. Spoiling is when other microbes, or the same ones for too long, make it unpleasant or unsafe.
explanations.description: Idli batter is left out overnight so that bacteria and yeasts can eat and multiply. They make gas, so the batter rises, and acid, so it turns sour. That is fermenting. Curd is made the same way, by curd bacteria. Because the good microbes fill the food first, they leave little room for harmful ones. But batter left out for two or three days goes too sour and may grow mould.
examples: Milk with a spoon of curd added sets into curd overnight.
Dosa batter rises when it ferments overnight.
Batter left out for three days smells too sour and may grow mould.
explanations.art: Two vessels of batter side by side: one risen and bubbly labelled 'next morning', one with a grey film labelled 'three days later'.
explanations.context: This card explains how fermenting and spoiling are both the work of microbes.

explanations.concept: Parts of food and their jobs
explanations.definition: Food is made of nutrients, and each kind has a main job in the body.
explanations.description: Carbohydrates, such as rice and ragi, give most of our energy. Fats, such as ghee and oil, give energy too, and the body stores fat for later. Proteins, such as dal, milk and fish, build and repair the body. Vitamins and minerals, such as those in fruit, leafy greens and milk, keep the body working and help it fight illness. Fibre helps food move through the gut, and water carries everything around. Microbes need many of the same nutrients. That is why the foods that feed us best, like dal and milk, also spoil fast.
examples: A ragi ball gives energy.
Sambar's dal gives protein for growing.
Amla and guava give vitamin C, which helps cuts heal.
explanations.art: A banana-leaf meal with each food labelled by its job: energy, building, protecting.
explanations.context: This card is about what food is made of, and why microbes like the same food we do.

explanations.concept: Food poisoning: what happens, and what to do
explanations.definition: Food poisoning is illness from eating food that has harmful microbes, or the poisons they made, in it.
explanations.description: Most food poisoning gives a tummy ache, vomiting or loose motions for a day or two. The body loses a lot of water, so the most important thing is to drink. ORS, a drink of clean water with the right amounts of salt and sugar, puts back what is lost. A child who cannot keep drinks down, or seems very sleepy, needs a doctor quickly. Some microbes make poisons that survive boiling. So reheating food that has already spoiled does not make it safe.
examples: A family at a wedding feast who all ate the same old chicken may all fall ill.
A child with loose motions drinks small sips of ORS often.
Spoiled dal is thrown away, not boiled again.
explanations.art: A glass of ORS on a table beside a sick child resting under a sheet, and a parent stirring a spoon.
explanations.context: This card explains what food poisoning is and what helps.

explanations.definition: The five-second rule says food dropped on the floor is safe if you pick it up within five seconds. Tests show microbes can move onto food in less than one second.
explanations.description: In 2016, Robyn Miranda and Donald Schaffner at Rutgers University in the United States tested it. They dropped watermelon, bread, buttered bread and jelly sweets onto steel, tile, wood and carpet spread with harmless bacteria. Some bacteria moved onto the food in under one second. Longer contact moved more. Wet watermelon picked up the most, and the dry sweet the least. So the floor, the food and the time all matter, and no rule of five seconds makes food clean.
examples: A wet cucumber slice picks up more floor dirt than a dry biscuit.
A clean, dry floor carries fewer microbes than a kitchen floor near the dustbin.
Food left on the floor for a minute picks up more than food picked up at once.
explanations.art: A watermelon cube and a dry biscuit on a tiled floor with a stopwatch beside them.
explanations.context: This card checks a popular idea about food dropped on the floor.

explanations.concept: How should we wash fruit and vegetables?
explanations.description: Everyone agrees that soil should be washed off, and that soap and washing powder must never be used on food. People disagree on whether soaking in salt water, tamarind water or vinegar water does much more than plain water.
examples: Many families soak greens in salt water before washing them.
Food safety agencies in many countries advise rubbing produce under clean running water.
Peeling removes more from a cucumber or carrot than washing does.

perspectives.who: Food safety agencies, such as the United States Food and Drug Administration
perspectives.explanation: Rub fruit and vegetables under clean running water. This removes most soil and many microbes. Soaps and special washes are not needed, and soap can stay on food and upset the stomach.

perspectives.who: Many Indian families and some researchers
perspectives.explanation: Soaking in salt water or a weak vinegar solution for a few minutes, then rinsing, removes more dirt and some pesticide from leafy greens. Some studies find this helps more than plain water. Other studies find only a small difference.

explanations.art: A bowl of greens soaking in water with a spoon of salt beside it, next to a tap with running water over tomatoes.
explanations.context: This card is about a question where people disagree: is plain water enough to wash vegetables?

agreed.text: Most food spoils because microbes, such as bacteria and moulds, grow in it.
agreed.evidence: Food that is boiled and sealed, so that no new microbes can get in, stays fresh for months or years. This is how tinned food works. Lazzaro Spallanzani showed this with boiled, sealed broth in the 1760s, and Louis Pasteur showed it again in the 1860s.

agreed.text: Microbes grow fastest in food that is warm and wet, between about 5 and 60 degrees Celsius.
agreed.evidence: Scientists grow microbes in labs at different temperatures and count them. Food kept in a fridge, or kept very hot, spoils much more slowly.

agreed.text: Boiling kills most bacteria, but not all spores and not all the poisons some microbes make.
agreed.evidence: Lab tests show that bacterial spores can survive boiling. Some outbreaks of food poisoning came from food that was cooked and then left warm for hours.

agreed.text: Washing hands with soap, washing produce, cooking well, keeping raw and cooked food apart and keeping food cold all lower food poisoning.
agreed.evidence: The World Health Organization's Five Keys to Safer Food are based on many studies of where food poisoning comes from.

agreed.text: Drying, salt, sugar and sourness keep many foods safe for a long time.
agreed.evidence: Microbes need water to grow. Dried, salted and sugary foods hold very little water that microbes can use. Pickles and dried fish have been stored this way for thousands of years.

challenging.claim: Food dropped on the floor is safe if you pick it up within five seconds.
challenging.who: A popular saying in many countries
challenging.for: Very little dirt can be seen on food picked up at once, and most people who do this do not fall ill.
challenging.against: In tests at Rutgers University in 2016, bacteria moved onto food in under one second. Wet foods picked up the most. You cannot see microbes, so 'it looks clean' tells you little.
challenging.context: This card is about the five-second rule for dropped food.

challenging.claim: If food smells fine, it is safe to eat.
challenging.for: Spoiled food often smells sour or bad, and a bad smell is a useful warning.
challenging.against: Some harmful bacteria grow in food without changing its smell or taste. Food left warm for many hours can make people ill even if it smells normal.
challenging.context: This card is about whether your nose can tell you food is safe.

challenging.claim: Boiling spoiled food again makes it safe.
challenging.who: A common idea in many kitchens
challenging.for: Boiling kills most bacteria, so reheating seems to start again.
challenging.against: Some bacteria make poisons that survive boiling. The poison stays even after the bacteria die, so food that has already spoiled should be thrown away.
challenging.context: This card is about reheating food that has gone bad.

challenging.for: Food lasts much longer in the fridge, so it seems the cold must kill microbes.
challenging.against: Cold slows most microbes but does not kill them. When the food warms up again, they start multiplying. Food in the fridge still spoils, only more slowly.
challenging.context: This card is about what a fridge really does to microbes.

challenging.claim: Packet milk must be boiled before drinking.
challenging.for: Boiling kills microbes, and milk can pick up microbes if it is kept out of the fridge, opened, or poured into an unclean vessel. Boiling is a safe habit when you are not sure.
challenging.against: Packet milk is already pasteurised. If it has been kept cold and the packet is fresh and unopened, it is safe to drink without boiling. Boiling for a long time also loses some vitamins.
challenging.context: This card is about a question families disagree on: should pasteurised milk be boiled?

big_questions.q: In your dabba test, the dal water spoiled because microbes were eating it. Was it 'spoiling', or was it someone's dinner?
big_questions.hint: Think about who was eating, and what they made as they ate.

big_questions.q: A boiled, closed dabba stayed fresh longest, but probably not for ever. Can any food be kept with no living microbes in it at all?
big_questions.hint: Think about tinned food, spores, and what happens the moment you open a tin.

big_questions.q: We call some microbes in food helpful, like curd bacteria, and some harmful. Do microbes care which group we put them in?
big_questions.hint: Think about what each microbe is trying to do for themself.

big_questions.q: Before fridges, how did your great-grandparents keep food for the rainy season?
big_questions.hint: Ask an elder. Think of vadams, pickles, dried fish, tamarind and jaggery.

big_questions.q: Food that feeds us best, like dal and milk, also spoils fastest. Why might that be?
big_questions.hint: Think about what microbes need from food, and what you need.

big_questions.q: Many families in India have no fridge. What would keeping food safe look like in their kitchen in May?
big_questions.hint: Think about cooking fresh, eating soon, boiling milk twice a day, and clay pots.

story.title: The Tamarind Rice Tin
story.note: The story is made up. The science in it is true: dry, sour, salty and oily foods keep longer, and cooked food left warm for many hours can make people ill.
text: The night before the long train journey, Paati's kitchen in Madurai smelled of tamarind and roasted chilli.
Kavya was nine. She and her little brother Arjun were going to Delhi with Appa, to see their aunt. The train would take almost two days.
"Two days of train food?" said Arjun.
"Two days of my food," said Paati. She was stirring a big pan of puliyodarai, rice mixed with a thick, dark tamarind paste, roasted dal, peanuts and plenty of sesame oil.

Kavya sat on the kitchen step and watched. On the counter were four steel tins. One held the tamarind rice. One held idlis rolled in milagai podi, the red chilli powder, with oil poured over. One held lemon rice. The last one held curd rice.
"Paati, why these four?" asked Kavya. "Why not sambar and rice, like every day?"
Paati smiled. "Good question. Sambar is lovely today. But by tomorrow afternoon, in a hot train, it would turn sour and frothy. These foods keep."
"Why do they keep?"
"You tell me," said Paati. "Look at them. What is the same about them?"

Kavya looked. The tamarind rice was sour and oily. The lemon rice was sour too. The idlis were dry and coated in oil and chilli powder. She tasted a grain of the tamarind rice. It was sour, salty and hot all at once.
"They are all sour, or dry, or salty," she said slowly. "And they all have oil."
"And the curd rice?" asked Paati.
"Curd is sour too," said Kavya. "But it is wet."
"Exactly," said Paati. "So the curd rice we eat tonight, for the first dinner on the train. The tamarind rice can wait until tomorrow."
Kavya remembered something from her science book. "Food goes bad because microbes eat it," she said. "Tiny living things. They need water and warmth. Sambar has lots of water."
"And tamarind?"
"Maybe sour is hard for them," said Kavya. "And salt pulls the water out of them. And oil keeps the air off."

Paati pressed the lid down on the tamarind rice tin. "My mother packed these same foods when she went to Kashi on the train, sixty years ago. She did not know about microbes. But she knew what keeps."
The next morning they climbed into the train at Madurai Junction. The fan turned slowly. Outside, the fields went by, green and then brown and then green again.
That night they ate the curd rice with a little lime pickle. It was cool and good.

The next day it was very hot. By lunchtime, Arjun was hungry and grumpy. Under his seat he found a small box. It was a little curd rice left over from the night before, shut in a bag all day beside the warm window.
"I want this one," he said, opening it.
Kavya held his hand. "Wait. That sat warm since last night. Smell it."
Arjun sniffed. "It smells fine."
"It might still have lots of microbes," said Kavya. "Some of them don't change the smell. Paati said wet food left warm for a long time is the risky one."
Appa looked up from his newspaper. "Kavya is right. Let's not take the chance."
Kavya opened the tamarind rice tin instead. It smelled just as it had in Paati's kitchen. They ate it with the peanuts crunching, and nobody missed the curd rice.
On the second evening, a man selling cut pineapple walked through the coach. The pieces sat on an open tray, and two flies walked on them. Arjun looked at Kavya.
"Uncovered, cut, wet and warm," he said. "Lots of microbes."
Kavya laughed. "Now you sound like Paati."

In Delhi, their aunt asked what they had eaten on the train. Arjun told her about the tamarind rice. Then he explained why it kept: sour, salty, oily and dry. Kavya let him tell it. He had worked it out on the train, and he got it right.
story.epiphany: For the parent: food keeps when microbes find it hard to grow in it. Dry, sour, very salty or oily foods keep for a day or more, while wet, mild foods like sambar or curd rice should be eaten within a few hours if they are not kept cold. Kavya worked it out by looking at what the travel foods had in common.
ask: What did the four travel foods have in common?
Why did the family eat the curd rice on the first night, and not on the second day?
Arjun said the old curd rice smelled fine. Why did Kavya still say no?
Why was the cut pineapple on the open tray a risk?
Which foods would you pack for a two-day train journey, and why?

games.title: Safe Kitchen: a snakes and ladders game
games.context: This is a board game like snakes and ladders. Food-safety habits are ladders, and risky habits are snakes.

printables.title: A 30-square board
items: Square 3, ladder to 10: You wash the coriander until the water runs clear.
Square 6, ladder to 14: You cover the rice with a plate so flies cannot land.
Square 9, snake to 2: You cut cooked chicken on the board that held raw chicken.
Square 12, ladder to 19: You put leftover sambar in the fridge after it cools.
Square 16, snake to 7: You leave cut fruit uncovered in the sun all afternoon.
Square 18, ladder to 25: You boil the milk and cover it.
Square 21, snake to 11: You eat a biscuit after playing outside, without washing your hands.
Square 24, snake to 15: You put a wet spoon into the pickle jar.
Square 27, snake to 20: You eat curd rice that sat in a warm bag since yesterday.
Square 30: Finish. A safe meal!

items: a tumbler

rules: Take turns to roll one die and move your token.
Landing on a ladder: read the square aloud, say why the habit is safe, then climb.
Landing on a snake: read the square aloud, say what the safe habit would be, then slide down.
If you can say the safe habit, you slide down only half way, rounded down.
On any square with a 5 in it, take a question card. A good answer moves you on 2 squares.
The first player to reach square 30 wins.

flow.kid: Safe habits are ladders. Risky habits are snakes. Say why when you land on one.

flow.do: Play the game. On each snake or ladder, ask for the reason.
flow.say: Why is that a snake? What would the safe habit be?
flow.kid: Why is it a snake? What should you do instead?

check.q: Lakshmi lands on square 24. She put a wet spoon into the lime pickle. Why is that a snake?
options: The water lets mould grow in the pickle
The spoon makes the pickle too salty
Wet spoons make pickle taste sweet
check.why: A pickle keeps because there is little water for microbes. A wet spoon adds water, and mould can start to grow.

flow.do: Talk about the game at the end.
flow.say: Which snake happens most in our kitchen? Which ladder could we climb this week?
flow.kid: Which snake happens in our kitchen? Which ladder can we climb this week?
flow.think: Is there a habit in our home that would be a snake on this board?

games.context: This is a quick game. A grown-up reads a food card, and you decide whether to keep it or throw it, and say why.

printables.title: A KEEP card and a THROW card for each player
items: KEEP
THROW

rules: Each player has a KEEP card and a THROW card.
A grown-up reads a food card aloud, without the answer.
Everyone holds up a card at the same time.
Each player says one reason. A right card with a good reason scores 2 points. A good reason alone scores 1.
Play until all the cards are read.

flow.do: Hand out KEEP and THROW cards. Read the first food card.
flow.say: Listen. Would you keep this food or throw it away? Hold up your card, then tell me why.
flow.kid: Keep or throw? Hold up your card. Then say why.
flow.context: This is the start of Keep or Throw?, a quick game about which foods are still safe.

flow.do: Read the cards one at a time. After each, ask for a reason.
flow.say: What would the microbes do in this food? Is it wet, warm, old, open, dry, salty or cold?
flow.kid: Think about the microbes. Is the food wet? Warm? Old? Dry? Salty?

check.q: A tin of food is bulging at the top. Should you keep it or throw it?
options: Throw it, because microbes inside may be making gas
Keep it, because tins keep food for years
Keep it, but shake it first
check.why: A bulging tin can mean microbes are growing inside and making gas. Some of them make dangerous poisons, so it must be thrown away unopened.

flow.do: Count the points.
flow.say: Which card was hardest? Why?
flow.kid: Which card was hardest? Why?
flow.think: Which food in our kitchen right now would you keep, and which would you throw?

experiments.title: Three Dabbas of Dal Water: which stays fresh longest?
experiments.question: Dal water is boiled and poured into three clean dabbas. One is closed, one is left open, and one is closed with an unwashed coriander leaf inside. Which one stays fresh longest?
experiments.predict: Before you start, guess. Which dabba will go sour and frothy first, and which will stay fresh longest? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: To make it fair, all three dabbas get the same dal water, boiled together, in the same amount. They are the same kind of dabba, rinsed the same way, and kept side by side on one shelf. Only one thing is different in each: whether it is covered, and whether an unwashed leaf goes in.

materials.item: half a cup of cooked toor dal or moong dal from the day's cooking
2 cups of water
3 small steel dabbas or steel tumblers of the same size, with lids or small steel plates to cover them
a pan and a ladle
a kettle or pan of just-boiled water, to rinse the dabbas
2 or 3 coriander leaves, straight from the market bunch, not washed
a strip of paper or tape and a pen, for labels A, B and C

experiments.safety: A grown-up does all the boiling and pouring. Never taste the dal water at any stage. Smell it by wafting the air towards your nose with your hand, not by putting your nose in. At the end, a grown-up pours it down the sink or toilet, and washes the dabbas with soap and hot water.

schedule.what: Guess, then boil the dal water, fill the three dabbas, and look at them at bedtime.
Look and smell, morning and evening, and fill in the table.
Look and smell again. Decide the order. Then a grown-up throws the dal water away and washes the dabbas.

experiments.record: Fill in the table with what you see and smell each time: clear or cloudy, bubbles or froth, a skin or fuzz on top, and the smell (fresh, a little sour, very sour). Then write what you think happened, what you saw, and why.

flow.do: 1. Show your child the three empty dabbas. 2. Explain what will go in each. 3. Ask for a guess and a reason, and write it down.
flow.say: All three get the same boiled dal water. A gets a lid. B stays open. C gets a lid, but first an unwashed coriander leaf goes in. Which will go sour first? Why?
flow.kid: Three dabbas, the same dal water. A is closed. B is open. C is closed with an unwashed leaf. Which goes sour first? Why?

ask.q: Which dabba do you think will stay fresh longest, and why?
good: A, because nothing new can get in.
A, because the leaf in C has dirt on it, and B is open to flies and dust.

flow.parent: Write the guess and the reason down, word for word. Do not say what you expect. Any reason is a good start.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Three Dabbas test. You find out which of three dabbas of boiled dal water stays fresh longest.

flow.do: 1. Mix the cooked dal and the 2 cups of water in the pan. 2. Bring it to the boil. 3. Let it boil gently for 5 minutes, stirring.
flow.say: Boiling kills most of the microbes already in the dal. So all three dabbas start almost clean.
flow.kid: A grown-up boils the dal water. Boiling kills most microbes in it. Stand back from the stove.
flow.parent: The mixture should be thin, like watery dal. If it is thick, add a little more water. Stir so it does not stick.

flow.do: 1. While the dal boils, pour just-boiled water into each dabba and onto each lid. 2. Swirl, and pour it away. 3. Label the dabbas A, B and C.
flow.say: Hot water rinses away most microbes inside the dabbas. We do the same to all three, so the test is fair.
flow.kid: A grown-up rinses each dabba with very hot water. Stick on the labels A, B and C.
flow.parent: Hold the dabbas with a cloth, as they get hot. Put the lids face down on a clean plate so nothing lands inside them.

flow.do: 1. Pour the hot dal water into the three dabbas, the same amount in each, about half full. 2. Close A at once. 3. Leave B open. 4. Drop the unwashed coriander leaves into C, then close it.
flow.say: Now only two things are different. B is open to the air. C has a leaf from the market, with whatever was on it.
flow.kid: A grown-up pours. A gets its lid. B stays open. You drop the unwashed leaves into C. Then close C.
flow.parent: Pick leaves with a little soil on them if you can. Do not touch the inside of the dabbas or the lids.

flow.do: 1. Put the three dabbas side by side on a shelf, away from the stove and the sun. 2. Do not put them in the fridge. 3. Look at them together at bedtime.
flow.say: They all sit in the same place, at the same warmth. Tonight they probably look the same. Let's write that down too.
flow.kid: Put them side by side on a shelf. Not in the fridge. Look again at bedtime.
flow.parent: Lift each lid only for a moment when you look, and put it straight back.

flow.do: 1. Morning and evening, lift each lid and look at the top. 2. Waft the smell towards your nose. 3. Fill in the table.
flow.say: Look for bubbles, froth, a skin on top or fuzz. Then waft the smell with your hand. Fresh, a little sour, or very sour?
flow.kid: Look at the top. Bubbles? Froth? A skin? Fuzz? Waft the smell. Write it down.
flow.parent: In a warm room, dabba C usually smells sour first, often by the next morning, with bubbles on top. B often follows by the evening of day 2, sometimes with a thin skin. A stays fresh longest. In a cool room, everything takes a day or two longer, so keep looking.
flow.wait: Day 2, morning and evening: look and smell.

flow.do: 1. Look and smell on day 3. 2. Write the order in which they spoiled. 3. Ask your child to say what they think, what they saw, and why.
flow.say: Which went sour first? Which stayed fresh longest? What do you think made the difference?
flow.kid: Which went sour first? Which stayed fresh longest? Why do you think so?

ask.q: Why do you think C spoiled first, if it did?
good: The leaf brought soil and microbes into it.
It started with many more microbes than A.

ask.q: Why might B have spoiled before A?
good: Microbes landed on it from the air and dust.
A small fly might have visited it.

flow.parent: If A also spoiled, that is a real result. A few bacteria make spores that survive boiling, and a lid on a dabba is not a perfect seal. Ask which spoiled first, not only which spoiled.

check.q: In the Three Dabbas test, Meenakshi's dabba C, with the unwashed leaf, went sour first. What does this show?
options: The leaf brought many microbes into the dal water
Coriander makes food sour by itself
Closed dabbas always spoil first
check.why: Dabba A was closed too, but stayed fresh longer. The only difference in C was the unwashed leaf. So the leaf added microbes, and more microbes means faster spoiling.

flow.wait: Day 3: look, smell and decide the order.

flow.do: 1. A grown-up pours all the dal water down the sink or the toilet. 2. Wash the dabbas with soap and hot water. 3. Everyone washes their hands.
flow.say: We never taste any of this. Spoiled food goes away, and the dabbas get a proper wash.
flow.kid: A grown-up pours it all away. Do not taste it. Wash your hands.
flow.think: Which food in our kitchen is most like dabba B, left open on the counter?

experiments.context: In this experiment you boil dal water and keep it in three dabbas: closed, open, and closed with an unwashed leaf. Over two days you look and smell to see which spoils first.

experiments.title: How Many Washes? The coriander test
experiments.question: How many washes does a bunch of coriander from the market need before the water stays clear?
experiments.predict: Before you start, guess. After how many washes will the water look clear? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: To make it fair, use the same amount of water each time, in the same bowl, and swish the leaves for the same time, 20 seconds.
results_table: Colour of the water (brown, light brown, nearly clear, clear)
Bits at the bottom (many, some, few, none)

materials.item: one bunch of coriander or spinach from a vegetable seller, with roots or soil on it
a big steel bowl
a white bowl, a white plate or a clear glass, to see the colour of the water
a measuring cup or a steel tumbler
a clock or a phone timer

experiments.safety: Use clean tap or filtered water. No soap on food, ever.

schedule.what: Wash the coriander again and again, pouring off the water each time, and count the washes until it is clear.

experiments.record: Fill in the table. Then draw a row of glasses, one for each wash, coloured from brown to clear.

flow.do: 1. Show your child the coriander bunch, and the soil on its roots. 2. Ask for a guess and a reason.
flow.say: Soil carries many microbes. How many washes will it take to get the soil off this coriander? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Look at the roots. See the soil? How many washes until the water is clear? Why?
flow.context: This is the first step of How Many Washes. You wash coriander again and again, and count the washes until the water stays clear.

flow.do: 1. Pour 4 tumblers of water into the big bowl. 2. Put the coriander in. 3. Swish it gently for 20 seconds, timed.
flow.say: Swish it gently, so the leaves rub against the water. Twenty seconds, then stop.
flow.kid: Put the coriander in the water. Swish for 20 seconds.

flow.do: 1. Lift the coriander out and hold it over a plate. 2. Pour a little of the water into the white bowl or glass. 3. Write its colour and the bits you see.
flow.say: Lift the leaves out first, so the soil stays behind. What colour is the water? What is at the bottom?
flow.kid: Lift the leaves out. Pour some water into the white bowl. What colour is it?
flow.parent: Lift the leaves out before pouring, or the soil settles back onto them.

flow.do: 1. Pour away the dirty water and rinse the bowl. 2. Repeat the wash with fresh water. 3. Keep going until the water in the white bowl looks clear.
flow.say: Same water, same 20 seconds. Is it lighter this time? How many more washes do you think it needs?
flow.kid: Fresh water. Swish for 20 seconds. Look again. Count the washes.
flow.parent: Most market coriander needs 3 or 4 washes. Coriander from a supermarket may already be cleaner, so it may clear in 1 or 2.

flow.do: Ask your child to say what they found, and why it matters.
flow.say: The water got clear. Do you think every microbe is gone now? What else do we do to coriander before it goes on food?
flow.kid: The water is clear. Are all the microbes gone? What else could we do?

ask.q: Is clear water proof that the coriander has no microbes left?
good: No. Microbes are too small to see, so some may still be on the leaves.
No, but there are far fewer, because most of the soil is gone.

check.q: After 4 washes, the water looked clear. What is most likely true about the coriander?
options: Most soil and many microbes are gone, but some microbes are still there
Every microbe is gone
The coriander is now dirtier
check.why: Clear water means the soil we can see is gone. Microbes are too small to see, so a few stay. That is why we wash well, and cook food when we can.

experiments.context: In this experiment you wash coriander again and again and count how many washes it takes until the water stays clear.

experiments.title: The Five-Second Test: does dropped food pick up dirt?
experiments.question: Does food dropped on a dusty floor pick up less if you lift it within one second? Does a wet food pick up more than a dry one?
experiments.predict: Before you start, guess. Will a wet cucumber slice or a dry biscuit pick up more turmeric? Will 1 second or 10 seconds pick up more? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: To make it fair, dust the plate the same way each time, drop each food from the same height, and press nothing down. Use a fresh patch of turmeric for each drop.
results_table: How much yellow stuck (none, a little, a lot)

materials.item: a big steel plate or tray, the darker and shinier the better
half a teaspoon of turmeric powder, our pretend dirt and microbes
a tea strainer, to sprinkle the turmeric
2 thin slices of cucumber, freshly cut and wet
2 plain dry biscuits
a clock or a phone timer, and a white paper plate to put the foods on after

experiments.safety: Turmeric stains clothes and fingers, so wear old clothes. Do not eat the test foods. A grown-up cuts the cucumber.

schedule.what: Dust a steel plate with turmeric. Drop a wet cucumber slice and a dry biscuit for 1 second and for 10 seconds, and compare.

experiments.record: Fill in the table. Draw each food after the test, colouring the yellow parts.

flow.do: 1. Tell your child about the five-second rule. 2. Ask for a guess and a reason.
flow.say: Some people say dropped food is fine if you pick it up within five seconds. Turmeric will be our pretend dirt. What do you think will happen?
flow.kid: Some people say dropped food is safe if picked up fast. Is that true? Guess first.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Five-Second Test. Turmeric on a plate is pretend dirt, and you drop foods on it to see what they pick up.

flow.do: 1. Sprinkle a thin, even layer of turmeric through the strainer on one side of the plate. 2. A grown-up cuts two thin cucumber slices.
flow.say: A thin layer is enough, like the dust on a floor. We need one patch for each drop.
flow.kid: Sprinkle a thin layer of turmeric through the strainer. Not too much.

flow.do: 1. Drop a cucumber slice flat onto the turmeric from about one hand's height. 2. Lift it off after 1 second. 3. Do the same with a biscuit on a fresh patch. 4. Put both on the white plate, face up.
flow.say: Drop, count one, and lift. Look at the side that touched. Which picked up more?
flow.kid: Drop it. Count one. Lift it. Look at the bottom. How much yellow?
flow.parent: Lift by the edges. Do not press the food down, because we want only what it picks up by itself.

flow.do: 1. Make two fresh patches of turmeric. 2. Drop the second cucumber slice and the second biscuit. 3. Leave them for 10 seconds, then lift.
flow.say: Now ten seconds. Do you think it will pick up more, or the same?
flow.kid: Now leave them for 10 seconds. More yellow, or the same?

flow.do: Compare all four foods. Ask what your child thinks, what they saw, and why.
flow.say: Which food picked up the most? Was 1 second enough to pick up some?
flow.kid: Which picked up the most? Was 1 second safe?

ask.q: Why do you think the wet cucumber picked up more?
good: Wet things are sticky, so the powder clings.

check.q: Anjali dropped a wet slice of cucumber on the kitchen floor and picked it up in one second. What is true?
options: Some dirt and microbes can stick to it, even in one second
Nothing sticks if you lift it within five seconds
Only dry food picks up dirt
check.why: In the turmeric test, the wet slice picked up yellow in one second. Scientists found the same with real bacteria: wet foods pick them up fastest, and some move across in under a second.

flow.think: Which floor in our home would have the most microbes on it, and why?

experiments.context: In this experiment you test the five-second rule, using turmeric on a steel plate as pretend dirt.

activities.title: Kitchen Watch: how does our family keep food safe?

materials.item: a sheet of paper and a pencil

activities.safety: Stay away from the stove and knives while you look.

schedule.what: Walk round the kitchen and find every way the family keeps food safe.

activities.record: A list with four headings: washing, covering, cooking, keeping cold. Add a fifth for anything else you find, like drying or pickling.

flow.do: Stand in the kitchen with your child. Ask what they notice.
flow.say: Food in our kitchen does not go bad straight away. What do you see here that helps keep it safe?
flow.kid: Look round the kitchen. What keeps the food from going bad?
flow.context: This is a short looking activity to start the unit. You find all the ways your kitchen keeps food safe.

flow.do: 1. Open the dabbas, the fridge and the cupboards together. 2. Write each thing you find under a heading.
flow.say: The lid on the rice tin, is that washing, covering, cooking or cold? What about the pickle jar?
flow.kid: Find lids, nets, the fridge, pickles. Write each one under a heading.
flow.parent: Good finds: lids on dabbas, a net or plate over food, boiled milk, the fridge, a dry spoon in the pickle, a separate fish board, sun-dried vadams.

flow.do: Ask what your child wonders.
flow.say: What do you wonder now? What would happen to the dal if we never did any of these?
flow.kid: What do you wonder? What if we did none of these?
flow.think: What is the food being kept safe from?

activities.context: This is a looking activity. You find every way your family keeps food safe, and sort them.

activities.title: Dust Catcher: what lands on uncovered food?

materials.item: 2 dark, clean steel plates of the same kind
a big steel bowl or a second plate to cover one of them
a torch or a phone light

activities.safety: No food is used, so nothing needs to be thrown away.

schedule.what: Wipe two dark plates clean and dry. Leave both on the kitchen counter, one covered and one open.
Shine a torch low across each plate and compare the specks.

activities.record: Draw both plates and the specks you see on each. Write which had more.

flow.do: 1. Wipe both plates clean and dry. 2. Put them on the counter, near the window if you can. 3. Cover one with a bowl.
flow.say: These two plates are like two plates of food. One is covered and one is open. What will land on them tonight?
flow.kid: Two clean plates. Cover one. Leave one open. What will land on them?
flow.context: This activity shows what lands on food left open overnight. You leave two clean plates out, one covered.

flow.do: 1. Next morning, take the bowl off. 2. In a dim room, shine a torch low and flat across each plate. 3. Count or compare the specks.
flow.say: Hold the torch low, almost flat. Dust shows up as bright specks. Which plate has more?
flow.kid: Shine the torch low across each plate. Which one has more specks?
flow.wait: Next morning: look with a torch.
flow.parent: The open plate usually shows many fine specks and perhaps a hair or an insect wing. Microbes ride on dust like this, but are far too small to see.

flow.do: Ask what this means for food.
flow.say: If that open plate had been dal, where would the dust be now?
flow.kid: If the open plate had food on it, where is the dust now?

check.q: In the Dust Catcher, the open plate had many specks after one night, and the covered plate had almost none. Why do we cover food?
options: To keep dust and the microbes on it from landing on the food
To keep the food warm for longer
To make the food cook faster
check.why: Dust settles from the air all night. Microbes ride on dust, so a cover keeps many of them off the food.

activities.title: Parts of Food and Their Jobs: sort your meal

materials.item: today's lunch or dinner, or pictures of the foods in it
a sheet of paper with three big circles drawn on it

schedule.what: Sort each food on a meal by its main job: energy, building, or protecting.

activities.record: Your three circles with each food drawn or written in the right one, and one sentence on what is missing.

flow.do: Draw three circles. Label them: energy, building and repair, protecting.
flow.say: Every food has a main job in your body. Some give energy, some build you, some keep you well.
flow.kid: Draw three circles. Energy. Building. Protecting.
flow.context: This activity sorts the foods on one meal by their main job in your body.

flow.do: 1. Name each food on the plate. 2. Ask which circle it goes in, and why.
flow.say: Rice, which circle? Dal? Ghee? The beans poriyal? Curd?
flow.kid: Put each food in a circle. Rice? Dal? Ghee? Vegetables? Curd?
flow.parent: Rice, ragi and chapati go in energy. Ghee and oil go in energy too. Dal, curd, milk, egg and fish go in building and repair. Vegetables and fruit go in protecting, for their vitamins, minerals and fibre.

flow.do: Talk about which circle is empty, and which foods spoil fast.
flow.say: Which of these foods would go bad first if we left them out? Why do you think the microbes like them?
flow.kid: Which of these would go bad first if left out? Why?

check.q: Which part of food mainly builds and repairs the body?
options: Protein, as in dal and milk
Carbohydrate, as in rice
Fibre, as in guava skin
check.why: Protein builds new skin, muscle and blood. Carbohydrates mainly give energy, and fibre helps food move through the gut.

activities.title: Read the Packet: dates and marks

materials.item: 3 or 4 food packets from the kitchen: milk, bread, biscuits, a masala packet
a magnifying glass, if you have one

schedule.what: Find the date, the storage advice and the FSSAI mark on each packet.

activities.record: A table with each packet, its date, how to store it, and how many days are left.

flow.do: Put the packets on the table. Ask your child to find the date on each.
flow.say: Every food packet has a date on it. It may say 'Best before' or 'Use by'. Can you find it?
flow.kid: Find the date on each packet. It may be tiny!
flow.context: This activity looks at food packets: their dates, how to store them, and the FSSAI mark.

flow.do: 1. Find the storage line, such as 'Keep refrigerated' or 'Store in a cool, dry place'. 2. Find the FSSAI logo and its number.
flow.say: FSSAI is India's food safety authority. Its mark and number show the maker has a licence. Which packets say keep cold?
flow.kid: Find FSSAI and its number. Which packets say keep it cold?
flow.parent: Milk and curd usually say keep refrigerated, and spoil within a few days. Biscuits and masala keep for months, because they are dry.

flow.do: Compare the dates.

projects.title: Make a Salt Lemon Pickle, and watch it keep

materials.item: 6 lemons
5 tablespoons of salt
half a teaspoon of turmeric powder
a clean, completely dry glass jar with a lid
a knife and a board, for the grown-up
a dry steel spoon

projects.safety: A grown-up cuts the lemons. Lemon juice stings in cuts and eyes. Keep everything dry: the jar, the lid, the spoon and your hands.

schedule.what: Wash and dry the lemons. A grown-up cuts them. Mix with salt and turmeric and pack into the dry jar.
Shake the jar. Look at how much juice has come out.
Shake the jar. Press a piece with the dry spoon. Is the skin softer?
Shake the jar. Look for any mould. Write what you see.
Taste a small piece with rice. Write how the lemons changed, and why no mould grew.

projects.record: A diary with one line for each check: how much juice, how soft the skins are, the colour, and whether any mould has grown.

flow.do: 1. Wash the lemons. 2. Dry them completely with a clean cloth. 3. Leave them for a few minutes to be sure.
flow.say: Water lets microbes grow. A pickle keeps because it has almost no water that microbes can use. So everything must be dry.
flow.kid: Wash the lemons. Dry them with a cloth. Every drop!
flow.context: This is the first day of a two-week project. You make a salt lemon pickle and watch it keep without a fridge.

flow.do: 1. A grown-up cuts each lemon into 8 pieces and removes the seeds. 2. Put the pieces in a dry bowl with the salt and turmeric. 3. Mix with a dry spoon.
flow.say: The salt will pull juice out of the lemons. Then the lemons sit in their own salty, sour juice.
flow.kid: A grown-up cuts the lemons. You mix in the salt and turmeric with a dry spoon.

flow.do: 1. Pack the pieces and all the salt into the dry jar. 2. Close the lid. 3. Keep it in a sunny or warm spot.
flow.say: Every day the salt pulls out more juice. Watch the jar.
flow.kid: Pack it into the jar. Close the lid. Put it in a warm place.
flow.parent: In many South Indian homes, the jar goes in the sun for a few hours each day. A warm windowsill works too.

flow.do: On days 2, 4 and 7, shake the jar and look. Write what you see.
flow.say: Is there more juice? Are the skins softer? Is there any mould?
flow.kid: Shake the jar. More juice? Softer skins? Any mould?
flow.parent: The juice should cover most of the pieces by day 4. The skins slowly turn soft and darker over two to three weeks.

flow.do: On day 14, take out one piece with a dry spoon and taste a little with rice and curd.
flow.say: Two weeks warm, no fridge, and no mould. What stopped the microbes?
flow.kid: Taste a little with curd rice. Why did no mould grow?

check.q: Revathi's lemon pickle stayed good for weeks without a fridge. What is the main reason?
options: The salt pulled water out of the lemons and out of any microbes
The turmeric made it yellow
The lemons were cut into small pieces
check.why: Lots of salt, and the sour lemon juice, make it very hard for microbes to grow. That is why the jar and spoon must stay dry: water would weaken the salt.

challenges.problem: The fridge has stopped working on a hot day. Plan how to keep a litre of milk from going sour until tomorrow morning.

a clay pot or a big bowl of water
general: Boil the milk, cover it, and boil it again in the evening and in the morning. This is how many families did it before fridges.
Set the covered vessel in a bowl of water, with a wet cloth over it, so evaporation cools it.
creative: Turn some of the milk into curd on purpose, so curd bacteria fill it before other microbes can.
Keep the milk in a clay pot with a wet cloth, in a shady spot with a breeze.
Make paneer from some of the milk with lemon juice, and use it the same day.

quiz.p: Why does cooked dal go sour if left out on a hot day?
opts: Microbes land on it, feed on it and multiply
The heat turns the dal into lemon juice
The dal absorbs sourness from the air
quiz.why: Microbes feed on the dal and make acid as they multiply. That acid is the sour smell.

quiz.p: Which of these does a lid on a dabba of food do?
opts: Stops new microbes, dust and flies getting in
Kills all the microbes inside
Makes the food cold
quiz.why: A lid keeps new microbes out. It does not kill the ones already there, and it does not cool the food.

quiz.p: What does a fridge do to the microbes in food?
opts: Slows them down
Kills them all
Makes them grow faster
quiz.why: Cold slows microbes down a lot, but most survive. When food warms up again, they start multiplying.

quiz.p: Why should cooked food not sit at room temperature for more than about 2 hours?
opts: A few microbes can double again and again into very many
The food gets too cold to eat
The food loses its colour
quiz.why: In warm food, some bacteria split every 20 minutes. After a few hours, a few have become millions.

quiz.p: In the Three Dabbas test, boiled dal water went into three clean dabbas: A closed, B open, and C closed with an unwashed coriander leaf. Which dabba usually went sour first?
opts: C, with the unwashed leaf
A, closed
They all spoiled at exactly the same time
quiz.why: The unwashed leaf added many microbes from the soil. Starting with more microbes, C spoiled fastest.

quiz.p: In the Three Dabbas test, boiled dal water went into three clean dabbas: A closed, B open, and C closed with an unwashed coriander leaf. Why were all three dabbas rinsed with just-boiled water?
opts: To keep the test fair, so all three started almost clean
To make the dal cook faster
To make the dabbas shiny
quiz.why: Rinsing all three the same way means the only differences are the lid and the leaf. That is what makes the test fair.

quiz.p: Which part of food mainly gives us energy?
opts: Carbohydrate, as in rice and ragi
Protein, as in dal
Fibre, as in guava skin
quiz.why: Carbohydrates, such as starch and sugar, give most of our energy. Protein builds the body, and fibre helps the gut.

quiz.p: Dal, milk and paneer are rich in protein. What is protein's main job in the body?
opts: Building and repairing the body
Keeping food cold
Making food taste sour
quiz.why: Protein builds new skin, muscle and blood, and repairs cuts.

quiz.p: Why does lemon pickle with lots of salt keep for months without a fridge?
opts: The salt pulls water out, and microbes cannot grow without water
Lemons have no microbes on them
The jar is made of glass
quiz.why: Microbes need water. Lots of salt pulls water out of them, and the sour juice slows them too.

quiz.p: Why do sun-dried vadams keep for a year in a closed tin?
opts: There is almost no water left in them for microbes
The sun turns them into stone
Microbes do not like the colour
quiz.why: Drying takes away the water that microbes need. Kept dry in a closed tin, they cannot grow.

quiz.p: Scientists at Rutgers University tested the five-second rule. What did they find?
opts: Bacteria moved onto food in under one second
Food was clean if lifted within five seconds
Only dry food picked up bacteria
quiz.why: Some bacteria moved across in under a second. Wet food picked up the most, and longer contact moved more.

quiz.p: Sudha, a girl in Kochi, says, "This chicken smells fine, so it is safe." It sat out all afternoon after a party. What is true?
opts: It may still be unsafe, because some harmful bacteria do not change the smell
It is safe, because it smells fine
It is safe if she eats it cold
quiz.why: A good smell does not prove food is safe. After hours in the warmth, harmful bacteria may have grown without any smell.

items.p: Dal left out overnight in summer smells sour and has bubbles on top. What is the main cause?
opts: Microbes are feeding and multiplying in it
The dal is drying out
The steel vessel is reacting with the dal
items.why: Microbes landed on the dal, fed on it and multiplied. As they feed, they make acid, which smells sour, and gas, which makes bubbles.

items.p: What do most microbes need to grow fast in food?
opts: Water and warmth
Light and cold
Salt and dryness
items.why: Microbes need water to take in food, and warmth to grow quickly. Cold, dryness and lots of salt all slow them down.

items.p: A fridge kills all the germs in food.
items.why: False. A fridge slows microbes down but does not kill them. Food in the fridge still spoils, only more slowly.

items.p: Washing coriander until the water is clear removes most of the soil and many microbes.
items.why: True. Soil carries many microbes, so washing it off removes many of them. A few microbes may still stay, because they are too small to see.

items.p: Heating milk for a short time and then cooling it quickly, so most microbes die, is called ________.
items.why: Pasteurising is named after Louis Pasteur, who heated wine in the 1860s to stop it going sour. Packet milk in India is pasteurised.

items.p: Match each habit to what it does to microbes.
pairs: Moves soil and microbes off the food
Stops new microbes landing on it
items.a: pairs as given
items.why: Each habit works in a different way. Together they keep the number of microbes in food small.

items.p: Sort these foods: which keep for months without a fridge, and which spoil within a day if left out?
items: sun-dried vadams in a closed tin
Keeps for months
sambar
Spoils within a day
lemon pickle in salt
Keeps for months
cut papaya
Spoils within a day
dry rava in a jar
Keeps for months
cooked dal
Spoils within a day
items.a: see items
items.why: Dry, very salty or very sour foods keep for months because microbes cannot get water or cannot grow there. Wet, mild cooked food spoils fast when left warm.

items.p: In the Three Dabbas test, boiled dal water went into three clean dabbas: A closed, B open, and C closed with an unwashed coriander leaf. Which one stayed fresh longest in most homes?
opts: A, closed with nothing added
B, left open
C, closed with the leaf
items.why: A started with the fewest microbes and nothing new could get in. B got microbes from the air and dust. C got many microbes from the soil on the leaf.

items.p: Put these steps for keeping leftover sambar safe in order.
items: Put it in the fridge
Let it cool for a short time, covered
Boil it well before eating it the next day
Pour it into a clean dabba with a lid
a: Let it cool for a short time, covered
Pour it into a clean dabba with a lid
Boil it well before eating it the next day
items.why: Cool it quickly, close it so nothing new gets in, keep it cold to slow microbes, and heat it well before eating to kill most of them.

items.p: Why do flies make food unsafe?
opts: They walk on rubbish, then carry microbes on their feet onto food
They eat all the vitamins in the food
They make the food cold
items.why: Flies land on rubbish and dirt, then on food. Microbes ride on their feet and mouths. A cover keeps them off.

items.p: Your friend Divya says, "I cooked this dal, so it is safe to eat tonight, even though it sat out all day." What would you tell her?
items.a: Cooking killed most microbes in the morning, but new ones landed on it, and a few survived as spores. All day in the warmth, they multiplied. Dal that sat out all day should not be eaten.
items.why: A strong answer says that cooking is not a one-time fix: microbes can multiply again in warm cooked food over many hours.

items.p: Why must the spoon you put in a pickle jar be dry?
items.a: A pickle keeps because it has very little water that microbes can use, and lots of salt. A wet spoon adds water, which can let mould grow.
items.why: A strong answer links the rule to what microbes need: water.

items.p: Draw dabba A and dabba C from the Three Dabbas test, as if you could see the microbes inside. Show which had more.
items.a: Dabba A with only a few microbes, dabba C with many, crowded round the leaf.
items.why: The drawing shows that the leaf brought in many microbes, and that more microbes at the start means faster spoiling.

items.p: Meenakshi and her mother Lakshmi disagree about packet milk.

views.says: We must always boil packet milk. Boiling kills microbes, so it is the safe habit.
Packet milk is already pasteurised. If it stayed cold and the packet is new, it is safe without boiling.

items.ask: Who do you agree with? Give a reason. Then say one thing the other person has right.
items.a: A strong answer picks a side with a reason, for example that pasteurised milk kept cold is safe, or that boiling is safer if the milk has been out of the fridge or poured into an unclean vessel. It also says what the other side has right.
items.why: Both have a point. Pasteurised milk kept cold is safe. But milk that has warmed up or been opened can pick up microbes, and then boiling helps.

items.p: Food that smells fine is always safe to eat.
items.why: False. Some harmful bacteria grow without changing the smell or taste of food. Food left warm for many hours can be unsafe even if it smells normal.

items.p: Some bacteria can split in two every 20 minutes in warm food. One bacterium lands on a bowl of curd rice. How many could there be after 1 hour?
items.why: 1 hour is 3 lots of 20 minutes. The number doubles three times: 1, then 2, then 4, then 8.

items.p: In the Three Dabbas test, boiled dal water went into three clean dabbas: A closed, B open, and C closed with an unwashed coriander leaf. In one home, dabba A also turned a little sour on day 3. What is the best explanation?
opts: A few microbes survived boiling as spores, or got in under the lid
Boiling makes dal go sour
Closed dabbas always spoil first
items.why: Some bacteria make tough spores that survive boiling, and a dabba lid is not a perfect seal. A still spoiled last, because it started with the fewest microbes.

items.p: In the Three Dabbas test, boiled dal water went into three clean dabbas: A closed, B open, and C closed with an unwashed coriander leaf. Why was it important to boil all the dal water together and rinse all three dabbas the same way?
items.a: So that only one thing was different in each dabba: whether it was open, or had an unwashed leaf. Then any difference in spoiling must come from that one thing.
items.why: A strong answer explains a fair test: change one thing, keep everything else the same.

items.p: Boiling spoiled dal again makes it safe to eat.
items.why: False. Some bacteria make poisons that survive boiling. Once food has spoiled, it should be thrown away.

items.p: Match each old way of keeping food to the reason it works.
pairs: Lemon pickle with lots of salt
Salt pulls water out of microbes
Lots of sugar pulls water out of microbes
items.a: pairs as given
items.why: All these ways make it hard for microbes to get water, or make the food too sour for them.

items.p: Sort each food into the part of food it is richest in.
items: ragi ball
Carbohydrate (energy)
toor dal
Protein (building)
ghee
Fat (stored energy)
rice
Carbohydrate (energy)
paneer
Protein (building)
coconut oil
Fat (stored energy)
items.a: see items
items.why: Grains like rice and ragi are mostly carbohydrate. Dal and paneer are rich in protein. Ghee and oil are almost all fat.

items.p: Dal and milk feed us well, and they also spoil fast. Why?
opts: Microbes need the same nutrients, such as protein and sugar, that we do
They are always cooked badly
They are heavier than other foods
items.why: Microbes feed on the same nutrients as us. Wet foods rich in protein and sugar, like dal and milk, are a feast for them.

items.p: A tough resting cell that some bacteria and moulds make, which can survive boiling and drying, is called a ________.
items.why: Spores let microbes wait through hard times. They are why boiled food can still spoil if left warm for a long time.

items.p: Put these in order, from the food that will usually spoil fastest to the one that keeps longest, all left out on a warm day.
items: Lemon pickle in salt
Cut watermelon
Dry rava in a closed jar
Idli batter
a: Dry rava in a closed jar
items.why: Cut watermelon is wet and sweet, with nothing protecting it. Idli batter is full of helpful microbes and keeps a day or two before going too sour. Pickle keeps for months, and dry rava for longer still, if it stays dry.

items.p: Arjun says, "Washing hands only matters if they look dirty." Use what you know about microbes to answer him.
items.a: Microbes are far too small to see, so clean-looking hands can still carry many. Washing with soap moves them off before you touch food.
items.why: A strong answer uses the fact that microbes are invisible, so looks cannot tell you.

items.p: Nandini's family washes greens in different ways.

views.says: Soak the spinach in salt water for ten minutes first. That brings out the dirt and the small insects.
Rubbing the leaves under clean running water is enough. Salt is not needed.

items.ask: Which way would you choose, and why? What test could you do at home to compare them?
items.a: A strong answer picks a way with a reason, and plans a fair test: the same amount of greens, washed each way, and the last rinse water compared in a white bowl. It notes that microbes cannot be seen, so the test shows only the dirt.
items.why: Studies differ on how much more salt water removes. Both ways remove soil. A good answer knows what a home test can and cannot show.

items.p: Draw a thermometer from 0 to 100 degrees Celsius. Colour the band where microbes grow fastest, and mark where a fridge and boiling water are.
items.a: A thermometer with the danger band from about 5 to 60 degrees coloured, the fridge below 5, and boiling at 100.
items.why: Microbes grow fastest between about 5 and 60 degrees. Food is safer kept colder than 5 or hotter than 60.

items.p: In the Five-Second Test, a wet cucumber slice and a dry biscuit were dropped on turmeric powder. What did most children find?
opts: The wet cucumber picked up much more, even in one second
Neither picked up anything in one second
The biscuit picked up more
items.why: Wet food is sticky, so the powder clings fast. Scientists found the same with real bacteria: wet watermelon picked up the most.

items.p: Cutting raw fish and then cucumber on the same unwashed board can carry microbes onto the cucumber.
items.why: True. The cucumber will not be cooked, so microbes from the raw fish stay alive on it. Use a different board or wash it with soap and hot water first.

items.p: Kavya, a girl in Madurai, packed tamarind rice and lemon rice for a two-day train journey, and ate the curd rice on the first night. Explain her plan.
items.a: Tamarind rice and lemon rice are sour, salty and oily, so they keep a day or more. Curd rice is wet and mild, so it was eaten first, before microbes could multiply in the heat.
items.why: A strong answer links each food to what microbes need, and why wet food is eaten first.

items.p: In the Three Dabbas test, boiled dal water went into three clean dabbas: A closed, B open, and C closed with an unwashed coriander leaf. Plan a fourth dabba that would show whether it was the leaf itself, or the microbes on the leaf, that made C spoil fast.
items.a: Dabba D: boiled dal water, closed, with a coriander leaf that was first dipped in boiling water for a few seconds. If D stays fresh like A, it was the microbes on the leaf, not the leaf.
items.why: A strong answer changes only one thing: the leaf is still there, but its microbes have been killed.

items.p: Two scientists argue about where the microbes came from in dabba B, the open one.

views.says: They fell in from the air, riding on dust.
A small fly visited it in the night and left them.

items.ask: Who do you agree with? What evidence would help you decide? How could you test it at home?
items.a: A strong answer says both could be true, and suggests a test: cover one open dabba with a fine net, which stops flies but not dust. If the netted dabba still spoils like the open one, dust and air are enough.
items.why: Good scientists design a test that separates two possible causes, instead of guessing.

items.p: Alice Evans, a scientist in the United States, found in 1917 that a bacterium making cows ill was almost the same as one causing a fever in people. What did she say should happen to milk?
opts: It should be pasteurised
It should be kept in the sun
It should be mixed with salt
items.why: She warned that raw milk from cows that looked healthy could make people ill. Pasteurising kills most of these bacteria.

items.p: Many doctors did not believe Alice Evans at first. Other scientists then tested her idea and found she was right. Why is it important that other people repeat an experiment?
items.a: One test can have a mistake, or bad luck. If other people get the same result in their own tests, we can be much more sure it is true.
items.why: A strong answer explains that repeating tests is how science checks itself.

items.p: Some bacteria double every 20 minutes. A bowl of cooked rice has 10 bacteria at 1 o'clock. If nothing stops them, about how many could there be at 3 o'clock?
items.why: 2 hours is 6 lots of 20 minutes. 10 doubles six times: 20, 40, 80, 160, 320, 640.

items.p: Put these in order of how fast they would spoil if left out, from fastest to slowest, and think about why.
items: Boiled milk, covered
Raw milk from a cow, open
Pasteurised packet milk, unopened, in the fridge
Boiled milk, open
a: Raw milk from a cow, open
Pasteurised packet milk, unopened, in the fridge
items.why: Raw open milk starts with the most microbes and gets more. Boiled milk starts with few, and a lid keeps new ones out. Cold slows them most of all.

items.p: A tin of food can stay good for years. Use the Three Dabbas test to explain how.
items.a: The food is sealed in the tin and heated hard enough to kill the microbes, including most spores. No new microbes can get in. It is like dabba A, but with a perfect seal.
items.why: A strong answer links heating and sealing, which together stop microbes being there and getting in.

items.p: Fermenting idli batter and spoiling dal are both the work of microbes.
items.why: True. In both, microbes feed and multiply. We call it fermenting when the microbes and the change are ones we want.

items.p: Why does a pressure cooker kill more microbes than an open pan of boiling water?
opts: It gets hotter, about 120 degrees, instead of 100
It cooks faster because it is heavier
It keeps out light
items.why: Steam trapped under pressure gets hotter than 100 degrees. The higher heat kills more microbes, even some spores.

items.p: Draw a comic strip of 4 pictures showing a microbe's journey from a dustbin to a plate of food, and one habit that could stop them at each step.
items.a: Four pictures, for example dustbin, fly, uncovered plate, mouth, with a stop such as a closed bin lid, a food cover, or washing hands.
items.why: Drawing the journey shows how microbes reach food, and that any habit that breaks the journey keeps the food safe.

items.p: Fermenting is when microbes we ________ change a food in a useful way.
items.why: Fermenting and spoiling are both microbes at work. The difference is whether we want the change.

items.p: In Kerala, many families dry fish in the sun before the rainy season. Why does dried fish keep for months, but fresh fish only a day?
items.a: Drying takes out almost all the water. Microbes need water to grow, so they cannot multiply in dried fish. Fresh fish is wet and full of protein, so microbes grow fast.
items.why: A strong answer names water as what is missing, and links protein to fast spoiling.

items.p: Sort these ideas: which are true, and which are myths?
items: A fridge slows microbes down
True
The five-second rule keeps food clean
Myth
Some microbe poisons survive boiling
True
Food that smells fine is always safe
Myth
Covering food keeps flies and dust off
True
Clear wash water means no microbes
Myth
items.a: see items
items.why: Each myth sounds sensible, but tests show otherwise: microbes move in under a second, some do not change the smell, and they are too small to see in water.

items.p: Match each part of food to its main job.
pairs: Keep the body working and help fight illness
Helps food move through the gut
items.a: pairs as given
items.why: Each part of food has a main job. A good meal has some of each.

items.p: A family has no fridge. It is May in Hyderabad. Plan their day of cooking so the food stays safe.
items.a: Cook fresh for each meal and eat it within 2 hours. Boil milk morning and evening and keep it covered. Keep pickles, dry snacks and dry grains for later. Wash vegetables well and cover all food.
items.why: A strong answer uses time, heat, covering and dry foods together, because there is no cold to slow the microbes.

applications: Dairies pasteurise milk before it goes into packets.
Tinned and bottled foods are heated and sealed so no microbes can live or get in.
Railway and school kitchens follow food-safety rules from FSSAI, India's food safety authority.
Hospitals cook food for patients with extra care, because illness makes people weaker against germs.
Ice cream, fish and vaccines travel in cold vans and boxes so they never warm up on the way.
Factories dry milk into milk powder and fruit into dried fruit so they keep for months.
Health workers teach families to boil or filter water, wash hands and cover food, to prevent diarrhoea in children.
Astronauts eat food that is dried or sealed in packets, because there is no fresh food in space.
